597213.old: Two acetyl-CoA molecules combine, in a reversal of the final step of β-oxidation, to produce acetoacetyl-CoA. The acetoacetyl-CoA reacts with another molecule of acetyl-CoA and water to form β-hydroxy-β-methylglutaryl-CoA, which is then cleaved to acetoacetate and acetyl-CoA. Most of the acetoacetate is reduced to β-hydroxybutyrate, while a small amount is decarboxylated to carbon dioxide and acetone.
597213.new: The figure below shows how they are made, and the table in the Lecture Connection classifies each step.

597214.old: Two molecules can play roles in moving it to the cytosol – citrate and acetylcarnitine. Joining of oxaloacetate with acetyl-CoA in the mitochondrion creates citrate which moves across the membrane, followed by action of citrate lyase in the cytosol of the cell to release acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate. Additionally, when free acetyl-CoA accumulates in the mitochondrion, it may combine with carnitine and be transported out to the cytosol.
597214.new: It travels as citrate: oxaloacetate and acetyl-CoA join in the mitochondrion to make citrate, which crosses the membrane, and citrate lyase in the cytosol splits it back into acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate.
597214.note: 15.6 conflict: two routes out of the mitochondrion (citrate and acetylcarnitine) vs. one in the Lecture Connection
597214.why: The Lecture Connection teaches only the citrate route (the citrate–malate shuttle), which is the route that supplies fatty acid synthesis; the acetylcarnitine sentence is cut so the page tells one story.

597214.old:
The fatty acid chain is built two carbons at a time (opposite of beta-oxidation), beginning with two acetyl-CoA molecules. One is converted to malonyl-CoA by carboxylation, catalyzed by the enzyme acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC). Next, both acetyl-CoA and malonyl-CoA have their CoA portions replaced by a carrier protein known as ACP (acyl carrier protein) to form acetyl-ACP and malonyl-ACP. Joining acetyl-ACP with malonyl-ACP releases the CO2 that was added and gives a four-carbon chain, acetoacetyl-ACP (see the figure in the Lecture Connection below).

From this point forward, the reaction types mirror those of beta-oxidation in reverse order, although the pathway is not beta-oxidation run backward (see the Lecture Connection). First, the ketone is reduced to a hydroxyl using NADPH. Next, water is removed from carbons 2 and 3 of the hydroxyl intermediate to produce a trans double-bonded molecule. Last, the double bond is hydrogenated to yield a saturated intermediate. The process cycles with the addition of another malonyl-ACP to the growing chain until a 16-carbon chain is reached and released as palmitate. At this point, the cytosolic synthesis ceases.
597214.new: The fatty acid chain is built two carbons at a time on an acyl carrier protein (ACP), using malonyl-CoA as the donor and NADPH as the reducing agent. Four reactions repeat (condensation, reduction, dehydration, reduction) until a 16-carbon chain is released as palmitate. The Lecture Connection below shows how the starting complexes are made and classifies each reaction.

597158.old: Alkaloid reagents, such as tannic acid (used in tanning leather)
597158.new: Tannic acid and similar polyphenols (used in tanning leather)
597158.why: "Alkaloid reagent" is an old name for reagents that precipitate alkaloids; students will not meet it elsewhere. The row keeps tannic acid, which is what the lab (Experiment 12) uses.

597158.old: These reagents combine with positively charged amino groups in proteins to disrupt ionic bonds.
597158.new: Their many –OH groups hydrogen bond to the protein, and they also bind positively charged amino groups, disrupting the protein’s own hydrogen bonds and ionic bonds so it clumps and precipitates.
597158.why: Tannins bind proteins mainly through hydrogen bonds from their phenol –OH groups (and hydrophobic contacts), not only through ionic bonds; the cell now says both.
